items.title: Adrian Ballinger Is Returning to Mount Everest’s South Side. Here’s Why.
items.summary:
For more than a decade, American expedition leader Adrian Ballinger swore off guiding climbers up Mount Everest’s popular South Col route in Nepal.

In interviews, Ballinger noted the crowds, the trash, the ever-present problem with human waste , and the frequency of rescues and deaths along the route. Atop his list of concerns, however, was the deadly Khumbu Icefall , the site of avalanches and dangerous crumbling seracs. Every spring, Sherpa porters and guides must make dozens of trips through the crumbling glacier to ferry food, tents, and oxygen to higher camps.

“If you run 20 trips on Everest over the next 20 years and hire 15 to 20 Sherpas each year, you’re putting a lot of people’s lives in danger,” Ballinger told Outside in a 2023 interview. “We don’t feel that we can run an ethical expedition from the south side.”

Ballinger’s company, Alpenglow Expeditions, led a handful of trips to Everest’s south side in the aughts. But starting in 2014, Alpenglow exclusively led Everest trips from the mountain’s northern side in Tibet, which is controlled by China.

Now, Ballinger is taking steps to return to Everest’s southern side. In a recent interview, he told Outside  that his three-year strategy for Alpenglow is to lead trips up Everest from both Tibet and Nepal concurrently.

“Even though we still think the north side of Everest is better for our clients, we are considering the south side as a backup,” Ballinger said. “And ultimately, we hope to be able to run trips on both sides of the mountain, provided we get the approvals that we expect.”

items.title: The Best Stretches to Reduce Quad Pain After a Hard Ski Run, According to a Physical Therapist
items.summary:
Having sore quads after skiing might seem like a side effect reserved for beginners who pizza their way down the slopes. But athletes of all levels can suffer from them.

Even with good form, your quads are the dominant muscle in skiing —especially the lateral quad (vastus lateralis), which is the most active when you turn, James Spencer , a physical therapist in Aspen, Colorado, told Outside . The stronger a skier you are, the harder you can push your quads on the mountain, which means “you can find a way to make them sore, no matter your skiing level,” he explained.

The root cause behind this soreness is the same reason your legs are tender after an arduous trail run or a lower-body weightlifting workout. When you intensely and repeatedly load your quads, you create microscopic tears in the muscle fibers. That damage may sound bad, but it’s actually a good thing: it’s one of the triggers that tells your body to strengthen that muscle, Spencer said.

Still, the side effects can be unpleasant. As with any bodily injury, the microtears trigger swelling, which increases the pain you feel after exercise and causes that sore sensation, Spencer explains. Officially known as delayed onset muscle soreness (DOMS), this feeling sets in after your workout ends and can peak as late as two to three days after. So if you feel fine boarding the shuttle at the end of a long ski day, but find yourself hobbling to the toilet the next morning, DOMS is probably the culprit.

The true cure for DOMS is time. “You really just gotta wait for those [microtears] to heal,” Spencer said. But…

items.title: The Forest Service Just Released Bigfoot Records Dating Back to the 1940s. Here’s What They Say.
items.summary:
In the 1940s, a man named Leo Kinney described in an informal written account a disturbing encounter along Petty Creek, a tributary of the Clark Fork River west of Missoula, Montana . At the time, he and three other hunters went into the woods to pack out a six-point bull elk they had shot down.

“On arriving where the elk was supposed to be lying, we found the entrails only, and in the snow coming to and leading away from the area was a large set of tracks,” Kinney wrote in his 1980 retelling.

At first, the men guessed a large bear had eaten the elk—but the tracks appeared in sets of two, and bears don’t tend to walk on their hind legs.

“Whatever it was had picked up the elk whole and clear off the ground,” Kinney continued.

The men followed the tracks for about a half-mile and, according to Kinney’s account, came across a felled log measuring three feet in diameter. They could see where the elk’s horns had been dragged across the snow and over the timber.

“At this point we held a conference and decided that we were not particularly anxious to catch up to whatever it was,” Kinney wrote. “Though we didn’t confess it at this time, in later conversations we found out that we all had a very uneasy feeling and could feel chills running up and down our backs.”

The following year, another person, W.W. Schmitz, was hunting in a nearby area called Bills Creek when he found the same type of tracks, smelled a similarly strong odor, and also heard grunting noises.

items.title: Officials Are Hunting for the Lake Tahoe Tree Killer
items.summary:
Authorities in Nevada are looking for a person who has been poisoning trees on the shores of Lake Tahoe . Since 2022, at least 28 pines have been harmed or destroyed, totaling $300,000 in damages, authorities said in a release.

Now, the Washoe County Sheriff’s Office (WCSO) and other local organizations are offering a $147,000 bounty to catch the culprit.

“We take these crimes very seriously and will utilize every available resource to identify and apprehend the person or persons responsible,” Sheriff Darin Balaam said in a statement . “The destruction of mature trees in the Tahoe Basin and the environmental damage caused by these deliberate acts are unacceptable.

In an email to Outside , WCSO spokesperson Rachel Piccinini said the agency is continuing to investigate the crimes, which could result in felony charges.

“Our office has received numerous tips from the community, and we continue to encourage anyone with information that may assist in this investigation to contact our Detective Division,” Piccinini said.

Outside  requested further information about whether the incidents pose a threat to people or pets recreating in the area. We will update this article if we receive a response.

(At least 16 trees were damaged in 2026 as a result of the most recent poisonings (Photo: Courtesy of WCSO)

items.title: Cut Off for 6 Years, Denali’s Only Road and Its Wildest Country Are Reopen for 2027
items.summary:
“Bear! On the left!” I jolt forward from the front passenger seat to find where our driver has spotted a grizzly on the open tundra. On a steep slope covered with birch trees, pops of autumn amber and rust scattered against green spruce trees, I can make out a moving boulder—then I spot its golden blonde fur. Olivia Juarez, general manager of Denali Backcountry Lodge , tells me it’s the signature coat of Denali grizzlies. Juarez is driving three of us, including her dog, on the entire 92-mile nearly unpaved stretch of the Denali Park Road, which feels precarious at times due to two-thirds of it being only one lane. But the speed limit is 35 mph, and we are the only ones on it.

For the last six years, this mostly gravel mountain corridor—the only road through Denali National Park and Preserve—has been closed after mile 43 due to a landslide. But in time for the 2027 summer season, access to the full 92 miles will reopen, allowing visitors to explore the depths of Denali’s backcountry once again.

Juarez slows the van to a stop, and we pass around binoculars. The grizzly is far in the distance, but it’s what surrounds it in every direction that catches my breath: striking volcanic cliffs in a kaleidoscope of earthy hues and gravelly, braided glacial streams stretching across an endless expanse of wild. It’s only us on the road, and this grizzly out yonder, for as far as we can see. And out there, somewhere hidden under a cloak of clouds, is Denali, or The Great One, as the peak’s traditional name translates from the Koyukon Athabascan language.

items.title: Matt Quinn of Mt. Joy Plays Acadia National Park
items.summary:
Mt. Joy frontman Matt Quinn has been visiting national parks his whole life. He’s found healing energy in nature and taken inspiration from the magic and fragility of places like the Maine coastline. So when we asked him to play Park Sessions in Acadia National Park , it was a natural fit. His music is in perfect harmony with nature’s stage.

During his visit to Acadia National Park with the Park Sessions crew, Quinn practices the art of slowing down—immersing himself in the Maine landscape, wildlife, and culture. He takes the winding roads around Mount Desert Island in the agile and spacious Mazda CX-50 , taking in the scenery as it changes from rocky coast to dense evergreen forest. Amid settings ranging from primitive skills lessons to beekeeping to lobster cookouts on the beach, Quinn’s set in Acadia is more than a performance—it’s a spiritual deep dive into what makes this park special. It’s a connection between music and the places that inspire it.

Explore Acadia Like Matt Quinn 
 Take a hike: From the Sand Beach parking area, take the Ocean Path Trail . This 2.2-mile out-and-back trail will take you to some of Acadia’s best-known highlights, including Thunder Hole and Otter Point.

Learn something new: Primitive skills instructor Mike Douglas taught Quinn how to start fire with a bow drill and how to feel his way through nature. You can hone your own outdoor skills through a variety of programs with the Maine Primitive Skills School .

items.title: A Hiker Fell off a Cliff in Big Bend National Park. Then Rescuers Had to Leave Him There Overnight.
items.summary:
A 19-year-old hiker is safe after falling off a cliff and staying the night on a narrow ledge in Big Bend National Park , one of the most remote national parks in the Lower 48.

According to a news release, on November 13, the man, whose name authorities have not released, fell ten feet when his gear gave way out in an area inaccessible to ground-based search and rescue responders. Rescuers reached the area just after 9 P.M. and called the Georgia Army National Guard medical evacuation crew assigned to the Joint Task Force-Southern Border. The organization works with U.S. Customs and Border Protection to monitor the shared border between Texas and Mexico, an area central to a heated national debate over the Trump Administration’s border wall construction .

The helicopter crew had taken off, but with limited lighting and winds approaching 35 miles per hour, and a string of storms moving into the area, the Black Hawk medevac crew made the difficult decision to scrub the mission.

“The crew agreed it was not safe and we had to make the unfortunate decision to go back and try again in the daylight,” Chief Warrant Officer 2 Gregory Hiett, the aircraft commander, said in a statement . “It was an extremely difficult thing to do, knowing the patient was going to be stuck out there for the rest of the night.”

Throughout the night, park responders remained on-scene and on the ground.

Just after 9 A.M. on November 14, a second helicopter mission launched with a hoist rescue team. Flight medic and technician Holly Johnson descended 150 feet on a cable, determined the hiker was…
